KEY MESSAGE 1...

Current IR satellite loop shows a large system organizing across the 
eastern half of the US. An upper level low is evident on the latest 
GOES-East 6.95um water vapor loop spinning into NW Missouri. Over 
the next 12 hours a surface low will develop off the South Carolina 
coast as another piece of upper level energy moves along the 
northern Gulf coast near the Florida Panhandle. By daybreak 
Thanksgiving morning a strong, well organized 994mb surface low is 
forecast to be centered over eastern North Carolina, moving north 
across Virgina through the morning and afternoon hours.

A large shield of rain and embedded thunderstorms will develop with 
this low, as a large influx of Atlantic moisture takes hold and 
PWATS reach 2.00 inches over the southern DELMARVA region. This 
influx of moisture will be supported by a highly anomalous 850mb low 
level easterly jet; on the order of 80-90 kts. The instability looks 
to remain south of the local area, but still cannot completely rule 
out some elevated rumbles of thunder getting close to our NE PA 
forecast area Thursday afternoon. A wind advisory has been expanded 
to now include all of NE PA and all east-Central NY. It is in effect 
from Thursday morning until 1 AM late Thursday night/early Friday 
AM. Peak easterly winds of 15-30 mph, with gusts of 45-55 MPH are 
expected in and around the advisory area...most likely Thursday 
afternoon and early evening. Forecast soundings from the 12z GFS 
show the 85kt jet at 850mb at AVP 21z Thursday, with winds potentially
mixing up to about the 925mb level...indicating potential gusts
of 40-55 kts down to the surface. The forecast soundings at BGM
show much of the same, but just a few kts lower. The peak winds
reach the Mohawk Valley area around or just after 00z Friday, 
showing the same 80kt jet at 850mb and potential momentum transfer
of wind gusts around 40-50 kts from the 925mb level. Winds at 
these levels can cause tree damage, scattered power outages and 
make for difficult driving conditions for high profile vehicles.

The steady moderate to occasionally heavy rain will advance north, 
reaching the Wyoming Valley area by 8-11 AM Thursday morning; then 
the NY/PA border by around 12-2PM. Can't rule out a very brief 
isolated pocket of freezing rain over the higher elevations of the 
Poconos or Catskills early in the day, but no impacts are expected.

The rain then reaches Penn Yan--Ithaca--Norwich and Oneonta by 2-4 
PM, and the I-90 corridor by 3-6 PM. The steadiest rainfall will 
occur from these start times until late Thursday evening or early 
Thursday night. It then tapers off to numerous/widespread showers 
Thursday night and Friday as the upper level low moves directly 
overhead. By the time rain completely ends Friday, totals should 
range from 0.75 to 1.50 inches, with localized amounts up to 2.00 
inches possible. This amount of rain is not expected to cause any 
significant hydrologic concerns. There could however be some ponding 
of water in low lying areas or roadways during the heavier rainfall 
rates (especially if storm drains are clogged with leaves or other 
debris).

The scattered showers continue into Friday night, gradually
tapering off and shifting further north on Saturday. With lows
above freezing Friday night and Saturday morning much of the
precip is expected to remain in the form of rain. If any wet
snow flakes do mix in from time to time, no accumulation is
expected for our forecast area.

KEY MESSAGE 2....

Although much weaker than the storm system impacting our area 
Thursday, another weather system is expected Sunday night into 
Monday. The low looks to track just west or right over the area 
early Monday morning with a period of rain likely. Temperatures will 
be mild in the mid-30s to lower 40s overnight, so it is expected to 
be all rain Sunday night. Some cooler air will gradually filter into 
the area on Monday behind the cold front, with 850mb temperatures 
falling to around -5C Monday afternoon. Some of the lingering rain 
showers could perhaps mix with some wet snow flakes later Monday 
into Monday into Monday night before ending. Temperatures will still 
be mild in the mid-40s to around 50 on Monday though. It cools off 
into the upper 20s to lower 30s by Monday night.

High pressure builds in from the west on Tuesday into Wednesday next 
week , so other than some lingering lake effect sprinkles or 
flurries on Tuesday it should dry out under partly sunny skies with 
seasonable temperatures.
